The June SEP projects **real GDP growth at 2.2% for 2026**, 2.3% in 2027, and the longer-run at 2.0%

**This is a late-cycle regime with stagflationary overtones.** 
The July payrolls print of -23,000 jobs — the first negative reading in several years — signals labor market deterioration
, while 
CPI spiked to 4.2% at its May peak as the Iran war drove crude oil sharply higher
.

The updated dot plot reflects a hawkish pivot, with fewer expected rate cuts signaled

the current +52 bp re-steepening from a -108 bp peak inversion historically precedes recession by 6–18 months
, a critical late-cycle warning flag.

The AI infrastructure investment boom remains the dominant earnings driver — consensus expects the largest hyperscalers to spend **$754 billion on capex in 2026**, an 83% increase from 2025.
 
Semiconductors, tech hardware, industrials, and utilities tied to AI power infrastructure are capturing the bulk of this earnings windfall.
 Energy equities are benefiting from structurally elevated crude prices — 
Brent crude is at $90/bbl and WTI near $84/bbl
 — with energy still up 14.7% YoY in CPI. Defense and aerospace are performing with geopolitical risk elevated. Short-duration fixed income (front-end cash, T-bills) remains a viable carry alternative at ~3.6%. **What's breaking:** Consumer discretionary and rate-sensitive sectors face a double-whammy of 
sticky shelter costs keeping real purchasing power compressed
 and 
gasoline at $4.04/gallon nationally
, squeezing the lower-income consumer. 
Long-duration bonds are under heavy pressure
, making REITs, utilities (ex-AI), and high-multiple growth stocks vulnerable to further multiple compression as the 30-year hits **5.25%** — a near 19-year high. Small caps face the tightest financial conditions given their floating-rate debt exposure.

**1. July PCE + Personal Spending (due ~Aug 29):** 
July PCE prices, personal income and spending, and durable goods data are all due imminently, along with annual nonfarm payroll revisions.

Concerns of unanchored inflation are being magnified by elevated energy prices during the U.S.–Iran blockade of tankers in the Persian Gulf.
 
Even under an optimistic scenario where the Strait closure lasts just one quarter, the oil shock is projected to raise U.S. headline inflation by 0.6 percentage points and core inflation by 0.2 percentage points in 2026.
 A re-escalation or extension of the conflict through Q4 would be the decisive variable in whether this regime transitions from late-cycle to outright contraction, and is the dominant tail risk to monitor daily.
